articles.title: Explosions hit Iran’s Qeshm Island as US media report US strikes in Hormuz
articles.summary: Several explosions heard on Qeshm Island and in Bandar Lengeh as US media report US military strikes in Hormuz.
articles.body:
Several explosions have been heard on Iran’s Qeshm Island, as media outlets in the United States reported that the US military carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.

The blasts came in rapid succession late on Monday, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast near the Strait of Hormuz.

The semi-official Fars news agency said explosions were also heard in the port city of Bandar Lengeh, coming from the direction of the sea.

The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that the US military carried out the strikes.

Some officials told the Journal the strikes were defensive, aimed at restricting Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. One official said Washington had deliberately kept the campaign quiet to avoid signalling a return to major combat operations.

The Associated Press news agency also cited a US official as saying the US had conducted defensive strikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz. The official said that “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets” had been targeted.

Reporters with Fox News and Axios said the attacks were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing at a US aircraft in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Citing a US official, Fox News reporter Jennifer Griffin said the incident did not mark “the start of expanded strikes by the US”.

There was no immediate comment from authorities in Iran or the US.

Earlier on Monday, the IRGC claimed it had captured two US drones, which it described as reconnaissance aircraft, south of Qeshm, using electronic warfare systems, and destroyed an MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The reported US attacks come on the eve of crucial midterm elections in the US, with US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party fighting to keep control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

They also come amid intensifying diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

Trump, writing on his Truth Social platform on Monday, suggested that a deal with Iran could happen soon.

“Oil Prices are dropping like a rock, down almost $10 a Barrel, a record, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran,” he wrote. “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!”

Earlier, when asked by reporters if he was considering striking Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump replied “no”.

US Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, expressed optimism about the negotiations before reports of the strikes emerged, telling reporters on Monday that he had discussed the talks with Trump earlier in the day.

“We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” he said when asked about a letter he sent last week to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei. “The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.”

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran’s demands for peace had been clearly communicated to Washington and “the ball is in the US court”.

He said Iran’s proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz had been condensed and could be implemented within two days if Washington met Tehran’s conditions. These included the US lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports and securing an end to hostilities, paving the way for the reopening of the strait and renewed negotiations.

Despite the diplomatic push, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also been pressing for another wave of strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, the Associated Press reported, citing two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.

articles.title: Greenland’s new airport is for tourists. But it could also support a future independent state
articles.summary: Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark.
articles.body: Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark. Thursday’s inaugural international flight between Copenhagen, Denmark, and Ilulissat, Greenland, was part of the island government’s efforts to grow its tourism industry to boost and diversify an economy still reliant on fishing. Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the new airport as “one of the biggest investments” in the island’s history. Nielsen was one of 169 passengers on Thursday’s 4.5-hour flight on an Airbus A330neo. An Associated Press journalist also took the flight, operated by government-owned Air Greenland, as part of a trip organized by tourism agency Visit Greenland, for this story. “If Greenland wants to be independent, we need to have a strong foundation, both economically and in terms of industry and business,” Nielsen told the AP before the plane departed. The strategic island, home to roughly 56,000 people, has been a focus of U.S. President Donald Trump since his first term, when he initially expressed his desire to acquire Greenland. His repeated threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally, during his second term prompted months of tensions with other NATO allies. In September, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. “There’s no doubt that it has been a shadow over the entire Kingdom of Denmark, but especially Greenland,” said Danish Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, who also took the inaugural flight. “The opening of this new international airport marks, I think, hope and optimism.” Ilulissat, known as the “City of Icebergs,” sits along the island’s western coast and is home to some 5,000 people. Greenland’s third-largest city is also one of the island’s most-visited destinations. More than 550 kilometers (342 miles) north of the capital, Nuuk, its tourism offerings range from sled dog tours to icefjord cruises in picturesque Disko Bay, known for its towering icebergs. Previously, travelers reaching Ilulissat had to arrive by cruise ship, take a small plane from Iceland or fly to one of Greenland’s international hubs and connect to smaller aircraft. There are no road connections from other big towns. For decades, Greenland’s main international aviation gateways were former U.S. military air bases, distant echoes of World War II, in Kangerlussuaq and Narsarsuaq. Locals and international visitors had to land there before catching smaller aircraft to the island’s major towns, including Ilulissat and Nuuk. That changed in late 2024, when an international airport opened in Nuuk.

articles.title: 'Calibrated non-kinetic measures': How Indian Navy foiled Somali pirates, rescued 20
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Indian Navy rescued all 20 crew members of a hijacked fishing vessel after carrying out a coordinated operation lasting more than 48 hours
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian Navy rescued all 20 crew members of a hijacked fishing vessel after carrying out a coordinated operation lasting more than 48 hours off the northeastern coast of Somalia. The operation involved a mission-deployed warship, a maritime reconnaissance aircraft, Marine Commandos and an Indian Air Force (IAF) C-17 aircraft.The Navy tracked the vessel, contained its movement and launched a tactical intervention to overcome the armed pirate threat, news agency ANI reported citing sources. All 20 crew members were rescued safely, with no casualties or injuries.The fishing vessel Azini had been hijacked by an armed pirate group earlier last month. The incident raised serious maritime security concerns, as the pirates could potentially have used the vessel as a ‘mother ship’ to launch further attacks against merchant ships operating in the region.The Indian Navy responded by deploying a warship and a maritime reconnaissance aircraft to locate and intercept the hijacked vessel. The operation involved sustained surveillance, coordinated tracking and the deployment of Marine Commandos to secure the vessel.How Indian Navy foiled pirate threatThe operation involved multiple stages, with naval and air force assets working together to locate the vessel, restrict its movement and eventually secure it.1. Warship and reconnaissance aircraft deployedFollowing the hijacking, the Indian Navy tasked a mission-deployed warship with intervening in the situation. A maritime reconnaissance aircraft was also deployed to provide aerial support.The two platforms worked in close coordination to locate Azini after persistent surveillance. Their tasks included:Locating the vessel: The warship and reconnaissance aircraft worked together to establish the location of the hijacked fishing vessel.Tracking its movements: The platforms maintained surveillance and monitored the vessel's movements to prevent the pirates from escaping.Restricting its movement: The Navy employed calibrated non-kinetic measures to contain the vessel and prevent it from moving away.The use of non-kinetic measures was an important part of the operation. These measures were intended to restrict the vessel's movement without relying on direct kinetic force. The Navy, however, did not specify the exact equipment or techniques used.2. Marine Commandos brought in through IAF C-17 aircraftThe operation was further strengthened with the deployment of Marine Commandos.The commandos were augmented through a precision airdrop carried out by an IAF C-17 aircraft. This brought together the operational capabilities of the Indian Navy and the Air Force.The deployment was part of the coordinated effort to secure the hijacked fishing vessel and overcome the armed pirate threat.3. Navy launches tactical intervention to secure vesselAfter locating and containing Azini, the Indian Navy executed a swift and coordinated tactical intervention.The operation culminated in the Navy securing the fishing vessel and overcoming the pirate threat.The intervention ensured that all 20 crew members were released safely. There were no casualties or injuries during the operation.The entire mission took more than 48 hours to complete.Why was hijacking of Azini a maritime security concernThe hijacking was not just a threat to the fishing vessel and its crew. It also raised concerns about the possibility of the vessel being used to facilitate further pirate attacks.According to the Navy, the pirates could potentially have employed Azini as a ‘mother ship’.A mother ship can serve as a base for pirates to operate farther out at sea. It can help them approach merchant vessels and launch further attacks.The possibility of Azini being used in this manner posed a wider threat to maritime security, particularly to commercial shipping operating in the region.By securing the vessel and overcoming the pirate threat, the Indian Navy prevented its potential use as a platform for further attacks.What did Navy sayNavy described the successful rescue as evidence of its operational preparedness and ability to undertake complex maritime security missions through coordination between the armed forces."The successful operation is a testament to the Navy’s high operational preparedness and ability to undertake complex maritime security operations through seamless inter-service coordination. It also underscores India’s unwavering commitment to remaining First Responder and Preferred Security Partner in the Indian Ocean Region," the Indian Navy said.The Navy also reiterated its commitment to safeguarding seafarers, protecting vital maritime trade routes and ensuring a safe, secure and stable maritime environment in the Indian Ocean Region.The operation highlighted India's role in responding to maritime security threats in the Indian Ocean and its efforts to protect seafarers and commercial shipping from piracy.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US to mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi next week, Witkoff says
articles.summary: Special Envoy Steve Witkoff announced the U.S. would be mediating upcoming Ukraine and Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week. “The United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia on November 10–11 in Abu Dhabi, advancing President Trump’s mission to end the war,” Witkoff wrote on the social platform X. “Discussions will…
articles.body:
Special Envoy Steve Witkoff announced the U.S. would be mediating upcoming Ukraine and Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

“The United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia on November 10–11 in Abu Dhabi, advancing President Trump’s mission to end the war,” Witkoff wrote on the social platform X . “Discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace.”

He continued that U.S. negotiators would meet this week in Brussels with France, Germany, U.K and NATO allies to “discuss security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s post-war security architecture, and economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction.”

“We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come,” Witkoff concluded.

The talks concerning Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine come as President Trump pushes to end the ongoing conflict.

First lady Melania Trump brokered a localized ceasefire in one Russian-occupied Ukrainian town that ended Sunday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky Monday said that Russia launched strikes that hit a humanitarian site. Reports state 26 people have died, with some victims still stuck under the rubble.

Current efforts to rescue people were hampered by Russian drone attacks in the affected area, according to the Associated Press , citing Mykhailo Semikin, a military official.

Zelensky warned in a post that Ukraine had “intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country,” which was targeting “energy and logistics.”

“The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked,” the Ukrainian president continued.

articles.title: Russian drone attacks turn the Black Sea into the world’s deadliest waterway
articles.summary: Russian drones have struck at least a dozen merchant ships in the Black Sea in recent weeks – killing more mariners than have died during the Iran war.
articles.body: Russian drones have struck at least a dozen merchant ships in the Black Sea in recent weeks – killing more mariners than have died during the Iran war. Russia’s goal is to throttle trade through Ukrainian ports, which export almost all the country’s grain. But some attacks have occurred close to or inside the territorial waters of two NATO states: Romania and Bulgaria. The Russian campaign follows months of Ukrainian strikes on ships using Russian ports in the Black Sea and adjoining Sea of Azov – and has accelerated over the past month. On several occasions, according to shipping and security sources, Russia has combined maritime and aerial drones. It has begun using recently developed jet-powered drones, which are faster and more difficult to intercept, as well as drones capable of hitting moving targets. Altogether, at least 30 mariners have been killed or are missing in the recent surge of attacks, according to maritime tracking services and the governments of Romania and Bulgaria. In the most recent strike, three drones struck a container ship last week as it approached a Romanian port. A French surveillance plane filmed a surface drone zeroing in on the vessel – the Contship Jet – and later video showed the ship listing heavily before sinking. When hit, the vessel was just 25 kilometers (15 miles) from the Bulgarian coast. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that the uptick in attacks is “turning the Black Sea into a zone of danger for civilian shipping.” Russia increased missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian Black Sea ports, particularly Odesa, over the summer. Ukraine exported 1.09 million tons of wheat in September, half the 2.05 million tons a year earlier, according to government figures. The Ukrainians tried to divert exports to smaller ports on the Danube River – which borders Romania – and Russian drones followed. The surge in attacks began in early October, when the Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading from Egypt to the Romanian port of Sulina, was struck by air and naval drones. Nine Syrian crew members and one Egyptian died, and the ship sank. Six days later, 11 of the crew on the HS Dignity – most of them Syrian – died when the ship was struck off the Bulgarian coast at night. A Syrian seafarers’ activist, Mohammad Hajjouz, told CNN that after the first strike on the Dignity, the crew saw an unmanned surface vessel approaching, which then struck the ship. Unable to fully launch the lifeboats, crew members jumped in the water. “They began calling out to one another and trying to regroup, but the sea was rough and the water was extremely cold, causing crew members to drift apart,” Hajjouz said. Despite the growing danger, some shipping firms are still working in the Black Sea. “Economic hardship pushes sailors to accept work in dangerous areas. They are sometimes enticed by offers of additional pay,” Hajjouz said. “Others are compelled to work in these areas due to limited employment opportunities.” On October 15, four more merchant ships were targeted, “including in Romanian territorial waters and its economic exclusive zone, and eight lives were lost,” according to Romanian Foreign Minister Oana-Silvia Toiu. Two chemical tankers – Wine Trader and Yara J – caught fire after being hit close to the Sulina Canal that leads from the Black Sea into the Danube. Six Beninese and one Russian national on the Wine Trader, which was hit by three drones according to its operator, were killed. “Russian forces are striking vessels linked to Ukrainian trade, now inside the (exclusive economic zones) of two NATO member states,” according to maritime analysts at Ambrey, a shipping intelligence firm “Romanian and Bulgarian waters should no longer be treated as safe by default,” Ambrey added, saying several vessels were very likely targeted due to their Ukrainian grain export links. Moscow has not acknowledged all the attacks, but in several instances the Russian Ministry of Defense claimed that targeted vessels were carrying “military and dual-use cargo” for the Ukrainian armed forces. A disjointed response The European response has been fragmented. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance has “already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank,” as Russian attacks encroach on the alliance’s borders. The Bulgarian government, which has relatively good relations with Moscow, has been reluctant to blame Russia, but there are now signs that it and Romania are mobilizing defenses. Bulgaria has asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defenses, according to Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, who also expects Bulgaria to join a NATO anti-drone initiative. The Romanians have begun deploying patrols of F-16 jets along the coast. One of them shot down two ⁠of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters in late October. Romania has also said it will accelerate the ⁠development of surveillance ‌capabilities and equipment to counter mines and drones in the Black Sea. But the moves have not done enough to reassure shippers. Traffic visiting Ukrainian ports has fallen sharply, while insurance rates have spiked. Last month, the Joint War Committee, which assesses risk for the London insurance market, extended the areas defined as “high-risk” to include the whole of the Black Sea region, excluding the territorial waters of Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia. Potential impact to global food system Higher premiums are bad news for Ukraine’s vital agriculture exports, 90% of which transit the waterway. Ukraine supplies about 15% of global maize exports and 10% of wheat, and is the world’s top exporter of sunflower oil. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has described the Black Sea as vital for global food security. But Russia “has put freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, and with it a lifeline for so many people, in its crosshairs,” he said last month. For its part, the Trump administration has blamed both sides for the shipping attacks. “We have American companies calling us and saying, ‘Hey, that was our oil on that ship that was hit by Ukraine,’” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month. “Now, I don’t believe Ukraine intentionally targeted them, but those ships got hit,” he added. NATO and the Black Sea states must “develop anti-drone defenses, and the Alliance should beef up its presence in Romanian and Bulgarian airspace and on land,” according to Dimitar Bechev, director of the Dahrendorf Programme at St Antony’s College at Oxford. “At sea, Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria could do more to enforce freedom of navigation,” Bechev told CNN. Ukraine and Russia are punishing each other without gaining any kind of lasting advantage, according to David Axe, author of the Trench Art blog on the conflict in Ukraine. That has left much of the Black Sea very perilous for commercial vessels. CNN’s Kosta Gak contributed reporting to this story.

articles.title: Greenpeace drops boulders in North Sea fishing grounds off Norfolk
articles.summary: Greenpeace drops nine large rocks to create a barrier to bottom-trawling fishing vessels.
articles.body:
Greenpeace has dropped nine boulders off the east coast of England to create a barrier that disrupts bottom trawling by fishing vessels.

The environmental campaigners' ship, Arctic Sunrise, sailed off the Norfolk coast to release the rocks without a licence over the weekend before mooring in Great Yarmouth.

Bottom trawling involves dragging weighted nets along the seabed to catch fish, although it can harm underwater vegetation.

Greenpeace claimed it had "effectively closed 116 sq km (45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA) to bottom trawling". The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said "activities at sea should be carried out lawfully".

When asked if they had permission to drop the boulders, Greenpeace said this was a "last resort" for it, and it did not have a licence.

It said that after years of meeting with politicians and the government to try to protect marine protected areas, progress had been "at a glacial pace".

A Defra spokesperson said: "We have strict legislation in place to protect our marine environment while supporting sustainable fishing and coastal communities.

"All Marine Protected Areas are safeguarded by legislation, with damaging fishing activities banned in more than 100 sites, and we are also considering further restrictions where there may be benefits in doing so.

"Activities at sea should be carried out lawfully and with due regard for the safety of other sea users."

Greenpeace added that bottom trawling could leave harbour porpoises , marine mammals which are found all over the UK's coast, with low fish stocks to feed on.

They added that the noise pollution of trawling disrupted the porpoises' ability to hunt and that the MPA had been designated to protect the animal.

After this, the government body responsible for managing coastal waters, the Marine Management Organisation (MMO), said: "As England's marine regulator, we are very disappointed that Greenpeace has chosen to take this action to drop boulders to form a barrier, as we don't believe it is justified or will help protect our marine environment."

Greenpeace said that after dropping the two-tonne boulders, it had called "the authorities to tell them the coordinates of each placement, and they update maps to inform other vessels".

The Southern North Sea MPA covers an area stretching from north of Dogger Bank (due east of Tyneside) to the Straits of Dover in the south.

articles.title: The zeptoverse: what is it and how will it transform physics?
articles.summary: Researchers have detected signals from the smallest distances ever probed.
articles.body:
Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.

A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.

The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.

The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.

'Knocking on the door' of the zeptoverse

Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.

"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.

But earlier this year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.

It did so as it announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope .

Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.

"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.

"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."

Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.

"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.

She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.

The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.

Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".

But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.

"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.

The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.

A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.

"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

articles.title: Reddit challenges Australia's under-16 social media ban, calls it 'ill thought out'
articles.summary: Australia's world-first ban on social media accounts for children under 16 is \"ill thought out\" and imposes a \"profound restriction on political debate\",
articles.body: Australia's world-first ban on social media accounts for children under 16 is "ill thought out" and imposes a "profound restriction on political debate", a lawyer representing Reddit told the country's top court during the first legal challenge to the legislation.Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group have approached the High court to challenge the law, which prohibits major social media platforms from allowing under-16s to hold accounts. The legislation came into force in late 2025, receiving backing from parents but facing opposition from technology companies.According to the news agency Reuters, a ruling against the law could encourage further legal challenges by affected platforms and potentially slow the adoption of similar restrictions worldwide. Countries including Britain and Malaysia are also pursuing measures aimed at safeguarding young people's mental and physical well-being.The Australian government and its communications minister, who has been named as a defendant, have said they will contest the challenge.Reddit argues ban restricts young people's voicesRepresenting Reddit, lawyer Perry Herzfeld told the court that preventing under-16s from maintaining social media accounts also denied them the ability to create or respond to content on what he described as the modern world's most important communication platforms."That is a very profound restriction on political debate in Australia," Herzfeld said, adding that the law placed a significant limit on what young people could do.He said Reddit supported the objective of minimising harm to young users but argued that the legislation was not an effective way to achieve it. Describing the law as "ill thought out" and "inept", Herzfeld said it did not prescribe specific measures to prevent minors from accessing platforms.He also argued that the restrictions failed to cover other online spaces where cyberbullying occurs, including gaming websites.Herzfeld pointed out that although posting or commenting on social media generally requires users to log into an account, a considerable amount of content remains accessible to people without one."If the Commonwealth is worried about particular features (of social media), it should regulate the features, which it has not done," he told the court.Australia toughens enforcement measuresSince the ban took effect, several studies, including research by Australia's eSafety Commissioner, have found that most teenagers below the age limit continue to access social media.In response, the government has doubled the maximum penalty for platforms that fail to comply with the law to A$99 million ($69.5 million). articles.title: London Museum launches food photography competition
articles.summary: The museum is collaborating with the World Food Photography Awards to showcase Londoners' foodie snaps.
articles.body:
A world food photography competition, which last year had nearly 9,000 entries from more than 50 countries, has added a new category to capture the diversity of London's culinary delights.

Organisers said they hoped images would be shared "which tell stories of how the city feeds itself - from Michelin-star restaurants to street markets, corner shops, delis, delivery bikes and soup kitchens."

The 'London Museum London Taste' category of the World Food Photography Awards is open to both amateur and professional photographers, wherever they live.

The launch comes as London Museum prepares to open its new home in Smithfield on 28 November, which has been central to London's food history.

The museum is restoring two former market buildings in an area which has been home to a market since medieval times.

London Museum director Sharon Ament said: "At our new home in Smithfield, food and drink will be part of how we tell London's story and bring people together.

"Food is an essential part of our daily lives, it can tell us a lot about people, places, attitudes, trends and values. The grit and glitter of our city."

Caroline Kenyon, founder of the World Food Photography Awards, added: "We want to see images of the people behind the vast and complex food system of the city, from delivery bikes to washer-uppers and chefs, as well as those shopping, cooking and eating."

The awards are open to professional and non-professional photographers, with 27 categories spanning everything from growing and harvesting, cooking and eating, to selling and celebrating.

Entries close on 7 February 2027, with all finalist photographs due to be exhibited at the Mall Galleries in London in May 2027.
